investigation.thought: No evidence yet, so start with an unfiltered metric_query that ranks every service and metric by deviation around the alert.

E1 shows the largest latency jump in productcatalogservice; recommendationservice likely calls it, so its latency may only be inherited. Comparing productcatalogservice's own latency with what its callers observe will show whether it is the origin.

Metrics (E1) and traces (E2) both implicate productcatalogservice, and E2 shows a 97.7x jump in caller-observed latency while its own self-time is flat, which points to network delay rather than CPU; its per-service metrics should confirm or rule out CPU/memory saturation before I settle the fault type.

Metrics (E1, E3) and traces (E2) independently point at productcatalogservice: its p90 latency rose about 844x while its own span self-time stayed flat (0.89x) and callers saw 97.7x latency, which fits injected network delay rather than a compute fault.

alternatives_rejected.why: Own span self-time is unchanged (p50 0.01->0.01ms, 0.89x) while caller-observed latency rose 97.7x (E2), so the extra time is spent on the wire, not in compute. No CPU deviation appears among the top metrics (E3).
The mem deviation (z=10.06, +50.3%) is tiny next to the latency deviations (z=16885 for p90, z=2792 for p50) in E3. A memory fault would also show up as higher self-time, which E2 does not show.

Its p90 latency rise (z=13770, E1) is smaller than productcatalogservice's (z=16885, E1). Calls into productcatalogservice rose 97.7x (E2), so recommendationservice's latency is consistent with waiting on that downstream dependency.

The huge error z-score (E1) appears alongside downstream latency explosions in productcatalogservice (E1, E3). Frontend errors are best explained as timeouts propagating up from slow productcatalogservice calls (E2).
